title: Wooden Indoor Environments' Restorativeness
research_question: To study the psychological effects of a wooden indoor environment on attention recovery and restorativeness.

participants.description: 48 students and staff members (24 females and 24 males, mean age = 37 years old, range 24–61 years) at the University of Padova (Italy). All were naïve as to the purpose of the experiment.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two identical real-sized rooms (341 cm (l) × 320 cm (w) × 260 cm (h)). One room (wood, W) was built entirely with wooden boards of Norway spruce (Picea abies L., Karst) and Silver fir (Abies alba Mill.). The other room (not-wood, NW) was built by applying fibre-cement flat sheets to a wooden framework and by plastering and painting both walls and ceiling, with vinyl boards (LVT) for the floor. Both rooms had a window, ceiling lighting, desk with chair, floor lamp, convector heater, and coat rack. White curtains provided privacy. Temperature, humidity, and luminosity were monitored to ensure similar environmental conditions.

Nine building material samples (11 cm x 16 cm pieces in white cardboard boxes with a 7 cm x 10 cm window for viewing and touching). Materials: light-colour spruce wood, dark-colour spruce wood, light-colour laminate, dark-colour laminate, light-colour wood-look ceramic, dark-colour wood-look ceramic, light-colour gres ceramic, white fibre cement, and dark-colour vinyl flooring.

measures.instrument: Semantic Differential Questionnaire (SDq) with 18 7-point bi-polar scales (e.g., complex-simple, unpleasant-pleasant, rough-smooth, cold-warm, artificial-natural, tiring-restorative).
Semantic Differential Questionnaire (SDq) with 21 7-point bi-polar scales (visual, tactile, auditory, olfactory, affective/evaluative items).

measures.construct: Sustained attention and attentional resources recovery
measures.instrument: Sustained Attention to Response Task (SART) measuring Correct Responses (CR), Incorrect Responses (IR), Mean Reaction Time (RT), and D-Prime (DP).

findings.mechanism: Not-wood environments do not provide restorative benefits for attention.

mechanisms: Wood's naturalness attracts involuntary attention (fascination), leading to a relaxing effect and recovery of attentional resources.
Multisensory perception of wood (visual, tactile, olfactory) contributes to feelings of pleasantness, warmth, and comfort.
Biophilia, the human innate tendency to focus interest on life and vital processes, explains the preference for wood and its beneficial effects.
moderators: Degree of biophilia of people involved in the experiments (mentioned in Demattè et al. [8] and referenced in this paper's discussion).
implementation_implications: Architects, builders, and interior designers should consider the positive psychological effects of wood when designing or renovating buildings, especially for work environments and homes.
Living comfort should extend beyond physical parameters (temperature, humidity, noise, luminosity) to include psychological well-being achieved through material choices like wood.

tables.description: Attention test experimental design (SART: sustained attention to response task; W: wood room; N: not-wood room). Shows the number of participants per group and the sequence of rooms for SART sessions and break.
Mean description (± standard deviation) of the different samples as a function of descriptor. Provides self-report ratings for nine building materials across 18 semantic differential scales.

Results of rooms evaluation using semantic differential questionnaire (ns: non-significant). Compares wood and not-wood room ratings across 21 semantic differential scales with t-statistics and p-values.

Mean number (± standard deviation) of sensitivity (DP), reaction times (RT), and correct and incorrect (errors) responses in Session 1 (before the break) and in Session 2 (after the break) for NNN, NWN, WNW, and WWW groups (N = not-wood room; W= wood room). Includes F-statistics and p-values for group differences and session x group interactions.

limitations: The involvement of a limited number of participants.
The study did not directly measure physiological indicators of stress reduction, which could further explain the effect of wood on stress reduction (as suggested by Ikei et al. [6]).
The study did not consider the biophilia level of participants as a moderator in the main attention experiment, only referenced previous work.

paper_metadata.title: Wooden Indoor Environments’ Restorativeness
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The sensitivity and interest toward well-being and health inside work and living environments is constantly growing. Wood is perceived as a natural material by people and its presence in a room generally induces beneficial effects on human beings. In this research, two real-sized identical wood and not-wood rooms have been built to study the psychological effects of a wooden indoor environment on attention recovery and restorativeness. After a multisensory evaluation of different kind of materials used in housing, participants were asked to evaluate the two rooms and then to perform an attention test two times, interspersed with a pause in one of the two rooms. The results show that wood samples are more appreciated than all other materials and that a wood environment induces an attentional resources’ recovery. These findings bring new insights in the interaction between human beings and indoor environments. This new knowledge should be taken into account in the design or renovation of buildings by architects and builders.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Humans possess an innate tendency to connect with nature and natural elements, which can lead to positive psychological and physiological benefits.
Environments containing natural elements can facilitate recovery from mental fatigue by engaging involuntary attention.
Exposure to natural environments can reduce physiological and psychological stress.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Restorativeness Scale (PRS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire measuring four components of restorativeness: Being Away, Fascination, Extent, and Compatibility.

instruments_used.name: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire measuring the degree to which situations in one's life are appraised as stressful.

instruments_used.name: Positive and Negative Affect Schedule (PANAS)
instruments_used.description: A self-report questionnaire consisting of 20 items to measure current positive and negative mood states.

mechanism_chain.description: Exposure to natural wood materials in indoor environments is proposed to enhance perceived naturalness and warmth, which in turn leads to reduced stress, improved mood, and increased restorative perceptions.

stimulus_images.description: Photos of the three experimental rooms used as stimuli: a room paneled with light-colour spruce wood, a room paneled with dark-colour pine wood, and a white-painted control room.
